title: Antiderivatives and the definite integral
note: An antiderivative reverses differentiation, and + C records that functions differing by a constant share a derivative. The definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx is a limit of Riemann sums, Σ f(xᵢ*) Δx: signed area, counting area below the x-axis as negative.

read.title: Adding up thin rectangles
text: How much area lies under a curve between x = a and x = b? Slice the interval into n equal pieces of width Δx = (b − a)/n. Over each piece, build a rectangle whose height is the function's value at some sample point. The total area of the rectangles, Σ f(xᵢ*) Δx, is a Riemann sum, and it approximates the area.

With only a few rectangles the estimate is rough. For an increasing function, rectangles using left endpoints sit below the curve and underestimate, while right endpoints overestimate. As n grows the rectangles get thinner, the errors shrink, and the sums approach a single number. That limit is the definite integral, ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx.

The integral measures signed area. Where f is negative, rectangle heights are negative, so that region subtracts from the total. This is why ∫₋₁¹ x³ dx = 0: the odd function x³ has equal areas above and below the axis that cancel.

Some integrals can be read directly from geometry. ∫₀¹ x dx is a triangle of area 1/2, and ∫₀³ √(9 − x²) dx is a quarter circle of area 9π/4. For most functions, though, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus offers a far faster route.
